polymarket-6937481.text:
But the _Needed_ column for the 1-month change (which represents the absolute value of the minimum change needed to be statistically significant at a 90 percent confidence level) is: 0.21

An official website of the United States government
The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the Employment Situation, or the “jobs report” every month, a news release that includes data from two surveys: the Current Population Survey (CPS) and the Current Employment Statistics (CES) survey.
The news release includes data tables from each: the “A” tables from the CPS and the “B” tables from the CES.
Each month, CPS publishes a set of statistical significance tables (XLSX) which correspond to each of the “A” tables in the Employment Situation, that is, summary table A and tables A-1 through A-16.
These statistical significance tables allow data users to determine whether seasonally adjusted estimates are statistically significant at a 90-percent confidence level compared to the prior month, or compared to 3, 6, 9 or 12 months prior.
For not seasonally adjusted estimates, the values to determine statistical significance are available for the prior month and 12 months prior.
To illustrate, see the image, below, of statistical table A-15.
The table includes: the estimates for the latest period (in this case it was May 2026); the 1-, 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-month changes calculated with more precision than appears on the “A” tables; a “Needed” column that provides the needed change for the estimate to be statistically significant at a 90-percent confidence level; and a “Statistically significant” column providing a “Yes” if the change was significant and a “No” if it was not significant.
Labor market indicators, such as the unemployment rate, are estimates produced from a sample survey.
Since a sample is surveyed, rather than the entire population, each estimate produced from the survey will have some level of error associated with it.
Sampling errors are differences between the results calculated from a sample of observations and those calculated from all observations in the population.
The statistical significance tables provide a data user the value for the confidence interval range around an estimate at a 90-percent confidence level.
Consider the following statement from the September 2025 Employment Situation:
...the unemployment rate, at 4.4 percent…changed little in September.
The unemployment rate in August 2025 was 4.3 percent
From the statistical significance tables, we observe the unrounded over-the-month change in the unemployment rate: 0.12
But the Needed column for the 1-month change (which represents the absolute value of the minimum change needed to be statistically significant at a 90 percent confidence level) is: 0.21
Thus, the one-month change in the unemployment rate from 4.3 percent in August 2025 to 4.4 percent in September 2025 was not statistically significant, and hence, the unemployment rate changed little over the month.
From January 2024 to March 2026, there were only two instances where the 1-month change in the national unemployment rate was statistically significant.
In the chart below, the shaded gray area represents a 90-percent confidence interval for each over-the-month change.
You can see that for most months, the change in the unemployment rate was within the confidence interval.
In order for it to be statistically significant, it needs to be the same value or greater than the bounds in the shaded area, as it is in February 2024 and July 2024.
Data users can assess statistically significant change over time for a variety of estimates found in the Employment Situation A tables, such as: estimates by nativity, educational attainment, veteran status, class of worker, reasons for unemployment, duration of unemployment, occupation, and industry.
The comparisons over time in the statistical significance tables are not adjusted for population controls.
Population controls are independent estimates of the population from the Census Bureau.
They are updated annually in the CPS, typically in January, and are used to weight, or control, the survey results to reflect the size and composition of the civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older.
Thus, in some instances, analyses in the Employment Situation news releases will be different from what appears in the tables, as the analyses determine statistical significance after accounting for population control effects.
Consider the following passage from the March 2026 Employment Situation:
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 59.2 percent, changed little in March.
These measures also showed little change over the year, after accounting for annual population control adjustments.
For the labor force participation rate, from the statistical significance tables, we observe the over-the-year change: -0.62
Based on the results in the table, it looks like the 12-month change in the labor force participation rate is statistically significant because the size of the change (0.62) exceeds the minimum change needed for significance (0.36).
However, the effect on the rate from incorporating the 2026 updated population controls was: -0.4
In order to remove the effects of the population controls, the effect must be subtracted from the over-the-year change: -0.62 – (-0.4) = -0.22
Thus, because the absolute value of the 12-month change after accounting for population controls was 0.22 and statistical significance requires a minimum change of 0.36, the 12-month change from 62.5 percent in March 2025, to 61.9 percent in March 2026 was not statistically significant.
At this time, the public cannot replicate estimates in the “Needed” columns because they are calculated using unpublished standard errors that account for the survey’s complex design in which households are interviewed multiple times.
These unpublished standard errors are calculated using the latest available data at the time of publication.
Data users can follow these instructions for calculating approximate standard errors for CPS estimates to calculate “Needed” values for 1- and 12-month changes in labor force indicators that will be close to those appearing in the statistical significance tables.
To access resources for determining the reliability and statistical significance of CPS estimates, visit the Reliability of Current Population Survey estimates page.
BLS has published standard errors in the Labor Force statistics database.
These standard errors provide measures of precision for CPS labor force estimates and facilitate comparisons with other estimates representative of the same time period.
To learn more about them, check out this factsheet.

A higher participation rate means a larger effective sample size for measuring unemployment, and a larger sample size reduces the standard error of the estimate.
Consider February 2022 and June 2025, which had very similar rates (unemployment of 3.9% and 4.1%, respectively, and a labor force participation rate of 62.3% for both months).
When the response rate declined 6.3 percentage points, from 73.7% in February 2022 to 67.4% in June 2025, the significance threshold rose from 0.18 percentage points to 0.21 percentage points.
This reveals that declining response rates do modestly reduce measurement precision.
However, the effect is relatively contained, and the CPS remains a reliable survey instrument despite these declines.
The Importance of Recognizing Sampling Variation
Understanding these statistical properties has important implications for interpreting economic developments.
The unemployment rate remains an essential indicator of labor market health, and the BLS statistical summary tables help determine which changes can be confidently attributed to genuine economic shifts rather than sampling variation.
When evaluating monthly unemployment data, it is important to recognize that single-month changes of 0.1 percentage points and even of 0.2 percentage points often fall within normal sampling variation and are thus difficult to interpret, while three-month cumulative changes provide stronger evidence of genuine trends.
Sustained movements over three months of at least 0.3 percentage points exceed the significance bands and thus provide much stronger evidence of true labor market shifts.
While declining response rates to the CPS have modestly reduced measurement precision, the effect remains manageable and does not undermine this fundamental approach.
Importantly, the BLS has consistently provided comprehensive documentation of measurement uncertainty and published statistical significance tests with every release.
Making full use of these resources provides a more complete assessment of labor market conditions than focusing on (changes in) the headline numbers alone.

US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
Department of Labor releases closely watched October 2026 jobs report
The U.S.
economy added jobs at a strong pace in October, rebounding from a softer September amid economic uncertainty.
What are the findings of the October 2026 jobs report?
The Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October.
That figure was well above the 65,000 estimate of economists polled by LSEG.
The unemployment rate decreased slightly to 4.1%, which was lower than the expectations of economists who predicted it would hold steady at 4.2%.
Revisions were made to the payroll numbers for the prior two months, with August revised up by 53,000 from a gain of 133,000 jobs to 186,000 jobs; while the change for September was revised up by 31,000 jobs from a gain of 29,000 to 60,000.
Taken together, employment in August and September was 84,000 higher than previously reported.
What sectors added or lost the most jobs in October 2026?
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 jobs in October, well above the 64,000 expected by economists polled by LSEG.
Government payrolls increased by 6,000 jobs in October.
The sector's loss of 17,000 jobs in September was revised down to a loss of 18,000 jobs.
The federal government shed 1,000 jobs in October, while state governments added 8,000 jobs and local governments cut 1,000 roles last month.
The manufacturing sector added 19,000 jobs in October, well above the gain of 5,000 that was predicted by economists polled by LSEG.
September's gain of 9,000 jobs was also revised up to 13,000.
Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs in October, which was well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 jobs over the past 12 months.
The sector's job growth was led by gains in professional, scientific and technical services (+32,900), and in administrative and support and waste management and remediation services (+28,100).
Healthcare added 41,600 jobs in October, above the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the last 12 months.
Most of last month's gains were in hospitals (+16,000), home healthcare services (+10,500) and outpatient care centers (+4,800).
Transportation and warehousing added 24,800 jobs last month, with growth occurring among couriers and messengers (+17,400) and air transportation (+3,500).
PRIVATE SECTOR ADDED 86,000 JOBS IN OCTOBER, ABOVE EXPECTATIONS, ADP SAYS
What does the October 2026 jobs report mean for the workforce?
The number of long-term unemployed, defined as those who have been jobless for 27 weeks or more, was 2 million in October and changed little over the month.
The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people.
The number of people employed part-time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October.
These individuals would've preferred full-time work but were working part-time because their hours were reduced, or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
The labor force participation was 61.9% in October, while the employment-population ratio was 59.3%.
Both of these figures were little changed in October and have shown little net change since January.
Average hourly earnings increased 3.1% year over year in October, above the 2.4% rise predicted by LSEG economists.
Earnings also grew 0.4% on a monthly basis, above the 0.3% estimate in the LSEG poll.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
What are experts saying about the October 2026 jobs report?
Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement that the October jobs report "is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown."
"Payrolls growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1%, and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions," Shah said.
"With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Lindsay Rosner, head of multi-sector fixed income investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that the October jobs report's "payroll number removed the traffic light at the December intersection for the Fed."
"Fed focus was already firmly on moderating inflation, and continued signs of tightening in the labor market give it a license to raise rates without hindering its employment mandate.
Additional tightening is possible in the first quarter if inflation continues to print strong," Rosner added.
What does it mean for interest rates?
The strong October jobs report raised the likelihood of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates when it holds its next meeting on Dec.
8-9.
The market's expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike ticked up on Friday, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 76.8% probability the Fed hikes in December – an increase from 66.9% a week ago.
A hike of that size would take the federal funds rate to a target range of 4% to 4.25%.

How did the market react?
The benchmark S&P 500 Index rose 0.65% during Friday morning's trading session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.25%.

Canada’s unemployment rate jumps to 6.7% as economy loses 4,700 jobs
Paula Tran
5 min read
Canada's unemployment rate jumped from 6.5 per cent to 6.7 per cent in October as the economy lost 4,700 jobs and more people searched for work.
Approximately 18,100 full-time positions were shed in October — a 0.1 per cent decline month over month — while part-time employment grew by 13,400 positions — a 0.4 per cent increase.
The latest Labour Force Survey data also showed 33,000 more people were looking for work, an increase of around 2.2 per cent month over month.
Most of the job losses were recorded in the services sector, which shed 25,300 jobs, a 0.1 per cent month-over-month decline.
Wholesale and retail trade took the biggest hit, losing 29,000 jobs.
Meanwhile, 20,600 jobs were added to the goods-producing sector.
Construction was up by 16,000 jobs and educational services added 15,000 jobs.
Overall, 52,500 private sector and 1,800 self-employed positions were lost in October, while the public sector gained 49,600 jobs.
October marked the second consecutive monthly increase in the unemployment rate, though it remains below the recent peak of 6.9 per cent in April 2026.
The employment decline was surprising for some economists, who expected the economy to add around 15,000 jobs in October.
Nathan Janzen, assistant chief economist for RBC Economics, said the monthly employment numbers were "extremely volatile" and the broader trends indicated that the labour market was slowly improving.
On a year-over-year basis, the unemployment rate was down by 0.2 percentage points in October.
"It was a little bit of a downside surprise, but if you look at the details, the employment declines were not broad-based," he said in an interview.
"This is against a pretty challenging economic backdrop for Canada with the U.S.
tariffs in place.
They're still significantly impacting a subset of the Canadian economy.
You're still seeing gradual improvement relative to that backdrop."
David Rosenberg, president of Rosenberg Research and Associates, raised concerns about the slowing wage growth.
Average hourly wages grew by 2.2 per cent year over year in October, following a 2.3 per cent increase in September and two per cent increase in August.
This is a slowing down from the 2.8 per cent year-over-year growth from July.
"When you're getting a slowing in the wage trend of this magnitude, it's telling you that the disinflationary output gap is widening," he said in an interview.
"The imported energy-induced inflation shock is creating the conditions for negative growth in real work-based incomes, which will then translate into negative trends on real consumer spending.
That is going to force the other components of the Consumer Price Index to deflate."
Both Janzen and Rosenberg said they're not concerned that Friday's report is indicative of the start of a trend because the month-to-month data is still too volatile.
However, the second consecutive rise in the unemployment rate is a signal that the Canadian economy is still fragile, despite showing signs of resilience throughout the year.
Rosenberg said there is a good chance that Canadian consumers will start to reduce their spending if the labour market continues to remain soft in the months to come.
"There's not a snowball's chance in hell that you're going to be getting a vibrant economy if the labour market isn't playing ball.
The reality is that the consumer is still the biggest component of the Canadian economy," he noted.
"This energy price shock hits the wall in the labour market, which means that it is a real income squeeze in the household sector, and a margin crimp in the corporate sector outside the resource patch."
RBC Economics' forecasts, however, projects that the unemployment rate will keep edging lower in Canada to below the six per cent mark in the second half of 2027.
Economic growth is also expected to slow from 3.3 per cent in the second quarter of 2026 to 1.8 per cent in the third quarter and 1.5 per cent in the fourth quarter.
"You're in that world where the economic backdrop is still fragile, and it's not a convincingly improving trend.
It's very gradual.
You will see some bouncing around along a very modestly positive trend line," Janzen said.
"It's more likely that as the economy continues to gradually improve, you would expect to see the unemployment rate edging lower rather than higher going forward."
Overall, Rosenberg and RBC Economics both expect the Bank of Canada to hold interest rates at 2.5 per cent in December.
RBC Economics expects the central bank to hike rates to 3.25 per cent by the end of 2027 in its most recent monthly forecast, while Rosenberg urged more caution from central bank governor Tiff Macklem.
Macklem previously told reporters that the Bank of Canada's governing council is going to consider the possibility of another rate hike one meeting at a time.
"It's going to take more than the shock that we've seen on the energy price front to generate a spillover into broad inflation with nominal wages slowing down as much as they are.
Tiff Macklem should realize that the odds of any energy spillover are minimal at best, judging from what's happening in the labour market and the visible slowing pattern in nominal wages," Rosenberg said.

OTTAWA — Some economists are getting worried that a string of job losses in recent months is revealing cracks in the labour market.
Statistics Canada said Friday that the unemployment rate rose two tenths of a point to 6.7 per cent in October.
The labour market shed 4,700 jobs last month, the agency said, and more people were also looking for work.
October’s modest decline followed a cumulative loss of 110,000 jobs across September and August.
A Reuters poll of economists had expected the economy would bounce back with a gain of 13,600 jobs in October.
“For anyone hoping that October would bring a recovery in the Canadian job market after back-to-back negative surprises, today’s release is a disappointment,” said Sneha Puri, economist with jobs search site Indeed, in a media statement.
Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions last month, marking the first decline in the segment since February.
Employment in the public sector, meanwhile, was up 50,000 positions.
StatCan noted that, on a year-over-year basis, private sector jobs are still up while the public sector is down.
Employment in the wholesale and retail trade industry has trended down over the past year and the sector led losses in October, shedding 29,000 roles.
Transportation and warehousing and food and accommodation also posted losses last month, offset by some gains in construction and education.
CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham said in an interview that he had expected more of a lift in the October labour market from one-time factors like the Alberta referendum.
While he had been anticipating the jobless rate would tick up in the fourth quarter in the face of tariff-related headwinds, Friday’s employment figures suggest there’s more underlying softness in the jobs market.
“It does look as if we’re seeing some weakness in the labour market outside of those trade-sensitive areas.
So that’s a concern for us right now,” Grantham said.
That could dampen expectations for a rebound in job growth in 2027, he added.
The unemployment rate for young workers aged 15 to 24 jumped to 13.7 per cent in October, up 0.7 percentage points from September, as employment edged down and more youth looked for work.
Young workers have faced a generally tough labour market in recent years but there had been little change in the jobless rate for the age group over the summer.
StatCan said the unemployment rate was higher for students compared with youth not attending school.
The agency said the layoff rate – the proportion of people employed in September who were laid off by October – was “virtually unchanged” compared with a year earlier at 0.7 per cent.
Average hourly wages rose 2.2 per cent annually in October, edging down from 2.3 per cent in September.
Puri said Indeed’s Canadian job postings ticked up at the end of last month, which could be an indication of future hiring.
If Canada can gain clarity on U.S.
trade policy in the wake of the midterm elections this week, she said that could give employers the confidence to hire again.
“If this optimism isn’t then translated into a strong jobs report in the months ahead, the surprising weakness in headline employment will start to look less temporary and more like the beginning of a renewed cooling in the labour market,” Puri warned.
The October job figures come a little over a week after the Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike in more than three years, raising its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent.
Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the uptick in the unemployment rate and muted wage growth should tell the Bank of Canada that there’s still slack in the job market right now.
The October jobs data should therefore push back on calls for much more tightening of monetary policy, he argued.
“Ultimately, this adds to our conviction that the bank will hike rates no more than twice more as a precaution against upside inflation risks, before calling it a day,” Ryan said.
Financial market odds of another quarter-point hike at the Bank of Canada’s final rate decision of the year on Dec.
9 stood at 35 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.
Bank of Canada officials made clear after the October rate hike that their focus is on getting ahead of inflationary pressures spreading from the global energy shock, Grantham noted.
Soft labour market data and recent declines in the benchmark price of oil take pressure of the central bank to deliver another rate hike next month, he said.
“We have a lot of days for oil prices to do something volatile between now and December.
But if those two forces stay in effect, we do forecast that they will hold interest rates at the December meeting,” Grantham said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov.
6, 2026.

Solana’s SOL token has fallen to its lowest levels since mid-August, trading near $75 in mid-November 2026.
The drop continues a multi-week slide that has erased roughly a quarter of its value over the past month and left the asset more than 70 percent below its January 2025 peak near $293.
Price action has tracked broader cryptocurrency weakness rather than any network-specific failure, with Bitcoin’s declines amplifying selling in higher-beta assets such as SOL.
Leveraged long positions were liquidated in waves as the wider market sold off, while large holders transferred substantial quantities of SOL onto exchanges, increasing near-term supply.
Sustained redemptions from Solana-linked exchange-traded products have removed a source of demand that had supported the token earlier in the year.
Institutional flows across major crypto ETFs have turned sharply negative.
Over the five trading days ending November 10, U.S.
spot crypto funds covering Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, XRP, Hyperliquid, and Zcash recorded combined net outflows of approximately $1.48 billion.
Bitcoin products absorbed the largest share at about $1.06 billion, while Ethereum funds lost $326 million; together they accounted for the bulk of the withdrawals.
Solana ETFs contributed roughly $47.4 million in redemptions, with XRP, Hyperliquid, and Zcash vehicles adding smaller amounts.
Bitcoin and Ethereum funds registered net inflows on only one session during the stretch, and Solana products have not recorded a single positive day since October 21.
Year-to-date through mid-November, Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs stand at a combined net outflow of roughly $2.25 billion, reversing earlier accumulation.
The pattern contrasts with renewed buying in traditional equity ETFs after an early-November equity selloff, underscoring a temporary divergence in risk appetite.Regulatory developments in China have added another headwind.
An unnamed official at the People’s Bank of China told the central-bank-supervised Financial News that authorities had halted planned offline events in the Solana Accelerate China 2026 series before they opened and would investigate the domestic entities and individuals involved.
The official described high-profile advertising in Shanghai’s Lujiazui financial district as virtual-currency marketing conducted through local partners.
SOL was characterized as essentially a virtual currency, and the network was noted for supplying technical services used in the issuance and trading of assets such as Tether’s USDT.
Both activities were said to fall outside permissions under a February 2026 multi-agency notice aimed at limiting virtual-currency risks.
The statements reaffirm Beijing’s continued restrictions on foreign public blockchains and related promotional activity, dampening any near-term expectation of policy relaxation.In a separate development, Stellar has recorded the strongest daily expansion in tokenized real-world-asset fund market capitalization among major networks.
Data compiled by the RWA Foundation from Token Terminal showed Stellar’s tokenized funds adding $44.9 million in the 24 hours through November 13, ahead of Solana’s $29 million increase,
Ethereum’s $10.8 million rise, and zkSync Era’s $3.5 million gain.
Stellar ranks second overall for tokenized funds behind Ethereum, with its broader RWA market value reaching approximately $4.67 billion after expanding roughly sixfold over the past year.
The network hosts Franklin Templeton’s BENJI money-market fund, which has operated on Stellar since 2021 as the first U.S.
mutual fund deployed on a public blockchain, along with products from Spiko, Ondo, and WisdomTree.
Compliance-oriented features have drawn traditional asset managers seeking tokenized Treasury and money-market exposure.
These concurrent trends highlight uneven conditions across blockchain ecosystems.
Solana faces concurrent pressure from macro-driven risk aversion, institutional redemptions, large-holder sales, and regulatory friction in a major market, while Stellar is capturing incremental institutional allocation in the tokenized-fund segment.
Whether the mid-$70s zone holds as support for SOL, and whether crypto ETF flows stabilize as broader financial conditions evolve, will be key near-term markers.

TL;DR: US spot Ether ETFs posted a $99.9 million net outflow on November 5, Farside data show, following an $85.3 million outflow on November 3 and a temporary recovery on November 4.
The pattern highlights a fragile demand picture, but cannot establish a direct forecast for ETH’s price.
Ether’s exchange-traded fund market is still searching for consistency.
The latest fully reported daily figures in Farside Investors’ Ether ETF table show a $99.9 million net withdrawal on Thursday, November 5, just a day after the same group recorded a $53 million inflow.
The reversal demonstrates why single-session data need context.
November 6’s table still contained unreported fields when reviewed, so it would be misleading to present the partial figure as a final market-wide total.
A dated, complete session offers a better basis for an editorial assessment.
On November 5, BlackRock’s ETHA recorded a $75.2 million outflow and the firm’s ETHB line showed a further $22 million leaving.
Fidelity’s FETH was down $2.2 million, while Grayscale’s ETHE showed a modest $500,000 withdrawal.
Those figures add up to the $99.9 million negative session.
The previous day looked different.
On November 4, the listed products collectively brought in $53 million, with positive flows in several funds offsetting negative readings elsewhere.
Before that, November 2 and 3 brought losses of $139.7 million and $85.3 million respectively.
The emerging picture is not a perfectly uninterrupted exodus.
It is a market in which intermittent buying has yet to overcome repeated bouts of selling.
Our earlier report on November 2’s Ether ETF withdrawals provides a useful baseline.
The subsequent sessions show that the pressure has persisted but has also varied substantially between days and issuers.
An ETF’s reported flow measures changes in the investment wrapper, not all Ethereum transactions.
Institutions can obtain ETH exposure through spot holdings, derivatives, treasury companies and other vehicles.
A negative day in the US listed fund category does not prove every sophisticated investor has turned bearish.
This is especially important for Ethereum because a significant share of the network’s economic activity occurs independently of an ETF.
Stablecoin transfers, decentralised exchanges, tokenised assets and staking continue to operate whatever happens to a particular fund’s share count.
The long-term investment case for ETH is often tied to that activity, but there is no automatic formula linking application usage to the token’s short-term price.
Concentration adds another layer.
If one manager dominates the day’s net withdrawals, the aggregate should not be described as a consensus of all issuers.
Analysts also need to separate price moves from flows: the dollar value of assets in a fund can fall because of market prices even when investors have not redeemed an equivalent amount of shares.
The first is whether ETF investors return in size and for more than a single session.
The second is what happens in Ethereum’s development roadmap.
The Ethereum Foundation announced a Glamsterdam testing delay on November 6, citing concerns about how proposed gas changes could affect existing applications.
That is an engineering issue, not proof of a market-flow response, and it should be covered on its own terms.
For traders and longer-term holders, the practical takeaway is to compare several fully reported sessions, assess which issuers are driving the moves and resist treating flows as a stand-alone trading signal.
Thursday’s number is meaningful evidence of weaker demand through US funds; it is not a reliable prediction of ETH’s next move.

Ethereum has extended its weekly decline as a multi-billion-dollar options expiry, institutional selling, and a hawkish Federal Reserve outlook have driven the token back toward its key $1,500 support.

- Technical indicators show bears remain in control, with $1,500 acting as the key support and $1,750 the first major recovery level.

According to data from crypto.news, Ethereum (ETH) fell about 7% to an intraday low of $1,517 on June 26 before stabilizing around $1,550 at press time.
The asset has dropped nearly 14.4% from its June 22 high of $1,773.
The selloff gathered pace after Ethereum lost its 200-day moving average near $1,668, triggering a wave of leveraged long liquidations.
Meanwhile, U.S.
spot Ethereum ETFs recorded roughly $260 million in net outflows this week, a sharp jump from the previous weeks, as institutional investors reduced exposure ahead of expectations for three Federal Reserve rate hikes this year.
Additional pressure emerged after the Ethereum Foundation announced a 20% workforce reduction and a 40% cut to its operating budget.
The restructuring raised fresh questions about the network’s development pace and funding outlook while traders were already navigating heightened volatility around the $11 billion options expiry.
Ethereum’s $1,500 support has become the market’s main test
Ethereum’s daily chart shows that the token has broken below the $1,805 support area, turning a former demand zone into overhead resistance.
The next major support sits near $1,414, while the current rebound attempt has remained limited after buyers defended the $1,500–$1,520 region.
On the four-hour chart, Ethereum has been moving inside a descending channel since its June 15 peak near $1,849.
The Fib retracement map places immediate resistance near $1,584, followed by $1,641, $1,681, and $1,720.
A stronger recovery would need a clean move above $1,750, which also matches a key level watched by traders.
According to analyst Ted Pillows, Ethereum’s momentum remains weak after retesting the lows.
“ETH tapped the lows again.
The momentum is still weak due to market correction.
But if Ethereum manages to reclaim the $1,750 level from here, we could see a relief rally next month.”
Momentum indicators remain soft.
The four-hour RSI is near 35, keeping Ethereum close to oversold territory without confirming a strong reversal.
The MACD remains below the zero line, although its histogram has started to flatten, showing that bearish pressure has slowed after the sharp drop.
The daily Aroon setup still favors sellers.
Aroon Down is at 100%, while Aroon Up sits near 21%, showing that Ethereum recently printed fresh lows while upside momentum remains limited.
The daily MACD also remains negative, with both signal lines deep below zero.
Liquidation clusters keep pressure on both sides of the trade
CoinGlass’ three-day liquidation heatmap shows heavy leverage around $1,590 to $1,610 and a larger cluster near $1,660.
If Ethereum rebounds through those zones, short liquidations could fuel a move toward $1,700 and then $1,750.
Below the spot price, the heatmap shows liquidation interest around $1,520 and $1,500 levels.
A break under that area would expose the $1,464–$1,414 region, where the daily chart shows the next major support band.
Whale positioning has also weakened.
CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost noted that three large Ethereum holder groups are now underwater, with unrealized profit ratios at -0.26 for 1,000–10,000 ETH holders, -0.21 for 10,000–100,000 ETH holders, and -0.05 for wallets holding more than 100,000 ETH.
According to Darkfost, this condition has not appeared since 2019, as even the largest Ethereum whales stayed in profit during the 2022 bear market.
The analyst added that Ethereum has remained “fairly resilient” despite the pressure, as similar whale stress periods have historically appeared near major bottom zones.
Downside risks remain high if Ethereum loses the $1,500 area with volume.
A daily close below that level would weaken the double-bottom setup and increase the risk of a deeper move toward $1,414.
A hawkish Federal Reserve, stronger U.S.
dollar, rising Treasury yields, and continued ETF outflows would add pressure if institutional demand fails to recover.
The bullish invalidation level is now clear.
Ethereum needs to reclaim $1,750 and then $1,805 to prove that the latest decline was a liquidity-driven flush rather than the start of another breakdown.
Until then, the market remains trapped between forced selling below $1,600 and short-covering risk above $1,660.

What is Ethereum?
Ethereum ranks as the second-largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, with a current valuation of around $233 billion.
It sits well behind Bitcoin’s roughly $1.33 trillion market cap but far ahead of the third-place option, Tether, at $183 billion.
Here’s what makes Ethereum different from other cryptocurrencies: It’s more than just digital money.
It’s actually a decentralized computing platform, which means users can build and run applications on it without any oversight from a company or bank.
Put simply, developers create apps on Ethereum’s blockchain network (rather than, say, Amazon or Google servers) to do things like borrow, lend, invest, trade, and more.
The token ETH serves as the currency you use to carry out those activities.
Ethereum price history
Ethereum’s initial coin offering (ICO) debuted in 2014 for just 31 cents per share.
Since that time, its value has increased by more than 60,000%.
From 2020 to 2025, Ethereum climbed by a still respectable 46%.
But that doesn’t capture the full picture.
Ethereum has experienced serious volatility, hitting nearly $5,000 at its peak in August 2025.
That’s nearly 1.6 million percent growth from its original ICO.
It makes that earlier 60,000% increase look pedestrian.
ETH has since posted gains exceeding 80%, losses surpassing 60%, and essentially every wild swing in between.
Early 2026 brought a sharp decline in Ethereum’s value for several reasons, ranging from recession concerns to Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin selling many millions of dollars worth of ETH.
The key takeaway is that Ethereum can generate massive gains and massive losses—about what you’d expect from other major cryptocurrencies.
Ethereum vs.
Bitcoin
After Bitcoin, Ethereum sits in a distant second place in the rankings for largest cryptocurrency.
But remember, Ethereum wasn’t originally created to function primarily as a currency; a decentralized computing platform was the main driving force behind its creation.
There are numerous real-world applications for Ethereum, and its developer community is massive.
Investors find this appealing because it has the potential to grow beyond being just an “alternative currency.”
Here’s a simple way to understand the difference between these two currencies:
- Bitcoin is often thought of like “digital gold.” It’s strictly a currency.
- Ethereum is like “digital oil.” It powers decentralized apps and contracts.
What is Ethereum staking?
Staking is another characteristic that distinguishes Ethereum from Bitcoin.
Until 2022, Ethereum’s network was secured by thousands of computers racing to solve random puzzles (called “proof of work”).
When your computer solved a puzzle, you’d receive some ETH as a reward.
It sounds odd (and it was), but it worked well for maintaining an honest account ledger.
Because this process consumed a lot of electricity and didn’t make much sense, Ethereum decided to abandon it in favor of an activity called “staking.” Staking is when you lock up your ETH as a security deposit to help validate transactions.
Doing so earns you a reward similar to what you’d get from proof of work.
You’re essentially earning interest on your stake.
What affects Ethereum’s price?
Many factors influence the price of Ethereum, including:
- Investor speculation: Like most crypto, Ethereum’s short-term price is heavily driven by trader sentiment and hype.
Speculative trading dictates price movements more than anything else in the near term.
- Network usage and decentralized finance adoption: When more people use Ethereum’s network, demand for ETH rises.
The decentralized finance (DeFi) boom of 2020-2021 was a great example of this.
- Economic health: Crypto isn’t as sensitive to interest rates as stocks, but the health of the economy still matters.
When people have money to invest, they’re more willing to explore alternative assets—like Ethereum.
- Regulations: Because crypto is still somewhat new, regulations are still evolving and major regulatory decisions can either scare or assuage investors.
- Competition from other blockchains: Ethereum isn’t the only “smart contract” platform anymore.
Competitors like Solana and Avalanche offer, in some cases, faster and cheaper transactions.
Depending on how Ethereum pivots will dictate its value in the long-term.

There are many ways to invest in Ethereum with varying degrees of risk.
Below are some of the most popular options.
Buy Ethereum on a crypto exchange
Purchasing ETH directly is the most hands-on investment approach.
Open an account with a cryptocurrency exchange and link your bank account to buy and hold the ETH in a digital wallet.
Invest in Ethereum ETFs
If you’d rather not manage crypto directly, including dealing with wallets and private keys, an Ethereum ETF might be a better fit.
These funds effectively hold the crypto on your behalf while their shares trade on stock exchanges like a regular stock.
Buy Ethereum-related stocks
Investing in publicly traded companies that are closely tied to Ethereum is a way to bet on ETH without owning it.
This could include blockchain tech companies, firms that hold a significant amount of ETH on their balance sheets, etc.
This lets you benefit from its performance by extension.
Open a crypto IRA that holds Ethereum
A crypto IRA lets you hold Ethereum in a tax-advantaged retirement account.
It works like a traditional or Roth IRA—with the same contribution limits and tax benefits.

This makes it overall less volatile than Ethereum, but it also lacks Ethereum’s potential for growth.

Is it a good time to invest in Ethereum?
Compared to blue-chip giants like Exxon Mobil or IBM, Ethereum is still pretty young.
There’s no foolproof way to predict how ETH will perform in the years or decades ahead.
Even so, its track record over the past decade has been outstanding, and its value goes far beyond being a tradable coin.
It’s the foundation for an expanding world of financial apps and developer tools.
Still, don’t forget that Ethereum has gone through some major downturns.
Be ready for volatility, and know it’s not ideal for investors who get uneasy with big price swings.
Keep an eye on competing blockchains, and don’t go all-in.
Treat ETH as a smaller, thoughtful piece of a well-diversified portfolio.

Ether ETFs shed $2.35 billion over seven weeks as investors trim exposure
Photo: Arturo Añez.
/ Pexels
US spot Ether funds have seen sharper and more persistent withdrawals than their Bitcoin counterparts, led by redemptions from BlackRock's ETHA
Investors have pulled $2.35 billion out of Ether ETFs over the past seven weeks.
That makes for one of the roughest stretches these products have had since they launched.
The more telling detail is how lopsided the selling has been.
Holders cut their Ether exposure more sharply than their Bitcoin exposure, which suggests the move is a vote on Ether specifically rather than a broad exit from crypto funds.
A record month, then more of the same
October did most of the damage.
US spot Ether ETFs posted $1.607 billion in net outflows that month, the largest monthly figure since the products debuted in July 2024.
Zoom out a little and the picture holds.
Roughly $1.65 billion left the funds during a five-week window that ended in late October.
November did not bring a turnaround.
Outflows across November 11 and 12 came close to $700 million, which means the selling carried straight through the calendar change.
The streaks are where it gets uncomfortable.
Ether ETFs logged nine consecutive days of outflows, a record for the products, and the research also points to a 23-day run of withdrawals during October.
Bitcoin ETFs, by comparison, swung back and forth between inflows and outflows over the same period instead of bleeding in one direction.

BlackRock’s fund carried most of the weight
If you want to know where the money left from, look at BlackRock.
The iShares Ethereum Trust, which trades as ETHA, accounted for 85% to 90% of withdrawals during the heaviest weeks.
ETHA alone saw $1.42 billion pulled in October.
That is most of the month’s record total coming from a single product.
Fidelity’s FETH went the other way.
It recorded modest inflows in October while the broader category was hemorrhaging capital.
How we got here
The outflows did not arrive out of nowhere.
Ether ETFs enjoyed positive inflows in August and September, and the October selling effectively reversed that run.
Meanwhile, Ether itself has been stuck in a range between $2,000 and $2,400 during the outflow period.
Context matters on the totals too.
Even after seven weeks of withdrawals, cumulative net inflows since the July 2024 launch stood at approximately $11.59 billion as of mid-November 2026.
That distinction is worth keeping straight.
Lifetime inflows measure how much new money has come in over time, while net assets reflect what is actually sitting in the funds today after withdrawals and price changes.
